function.name: todowrite
function.description:
Create and maintain a structured task list for the current coding session. Tracks progress, organizes multi-step work, and surfaces status to the user.

## When to use
Use proactively when:
- The task requires 3+ distinct steps or actions (not just 3 tool calls for a single conceptual step)
- The work is non-trivial and benefits from planning
- The user provides multiple tasks (numbered or comma-separated) or explicitly asks for a todo list
- New instructions arrive - capture them as todos
- You start a task - mark it `in_progress` (only one at a time) before working
- You finish a task - mark it `completed` and add any follow-ups discovered during the work

## When NOT to use
Skip when:
- The work is a single, straightforward task (or <3 trivial steps)
- The request is purely informational or conversational
- Tracking adds no organizational value

## States
- `pending` - not started
- `in_progress` - actively working (exactly ONE at a time)
- `completed` - finished successfully
- `cancelled` - no longer needed

## Rules
- Update status in real time; don't batch completions
- Mark `completed` only after the required work is actually done, including any required verification. Never based on intent.
- Keep exactly one `in_progress` while work remains
- If blocked or partial, keep it `in_progress` and add a follow-up todo describing the blocker
- Preserve user-provided commands verbatim (flags, args, order)
- Items should be specific and actionable; break large work into smaller steps

## Examples

Use it:
- "Add a dark mode toggle and run the tests" -> multi-step feature + explicit verification
- "Rename getCwd -> getCurrentWorkingDirectory across the repo" -> grep reveals 15 occurrences in 8 files
- "Implement registration, catalog, cart, checkout" -> multiple complex features

Skip it:
- "How do I print Hello World in Python?" -> informational
- "Add a comment to calculateTotal" -> single edit
- "Run npm install and tell me what happened" -> one command

When in doubt, use it.

function.name: todowrite
function.description:
Create and maintain a structured task list for the current coding session. Tracks progress, organizes multi-step work, and surfaces status to the user.

## When to use
Use proactively when:
- The task requires 3+ distinct steps or actions (not just 3 tool calls for a single conceptual step)
- The work is non-trivial and benefits from planning
- The user provides multiple tasks (numbered or comma-separated) or explicitly asks for a todo list
- New instructions arrive - capture them as todos
- You start a task - mark it `in_progress` (only one at a time) before working
- You finish a task - mark it `completed` and add any follow-ups discovered during the work

## When NOT to use
Skip when:
- The work is a single, straightforward task (or <3 trivial steps)
- The request is purely informational or conversational
- Tracking adds no organizational value

## States
- `pending` - not started
- `in_progress` - actively working (exactly ONE at a time)
- `completed` - finished successfully
- `cancelled` - no longer needed

## Rules
- Update status in real time; don't batch completions
- Mark `completed` only after the required work is actually done, including any required verification. Never based on intent.
- Keep exactly one `in_progress` while work remains
- If blocked or partial, keep it `in_progress` and add a follow-up todo describing the blocker
- Preserve user-provided commands verbatim (flags, args, order)
- Items should be specific and actionable; break large work into smaller steps

## Examples

Use it:
- "Add a dark mode toggle and run the tests" -> multi-step feature + explicit verification
- "Rename getCwd -> getCurrentWorkingDirectory across the repo" -> grep reveals 15 occurrences in 8 files
- "Implement registration, catalog, cart, checkout" -> multiple complex features

Skip it:
- "How do I print Hello World in Python?" -> informational
- "Add a comment to calculateTotal" -> single edit
- "Run npm install and tell me what happened" -> one command

When in doubt, use it.

content.description: Brief description of the task

status.description: Current status of the task: pending, in_progress, completed, cancelled

priority.description: Priority level of the task: high, medium, low

</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

function.name: bash
function.description:
Executes a given bash command in a persistent shell session with optional timeout, ensuring proper handling and security measures.

Be aware: OS: darwin, Shell: zsh

All commands run in the current working directory by default. Use the `workdir` parameter if you need to run a command in a different directory. AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>` patterns - use `workdir` instead.

Use `/var/folders/s2/xhvz8b6x44s6_5hs56kkxk2c0000gn/T/opencode` for temporary work outside the workspace. This directory has already been created, already exists, and is pre-approved for external directory access.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations like git, npm, docker, etc. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location
   - For example, before running "mkdir foo/bar", first use `ls foo` to check that "foo" exists and is the intended parent directory

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes (e.g., rm "path with spaces/file.txt")
   - Examples of proper quoting:
     - mkdir "/Users/name/My Documents" (correct)
     - mkdir /Users/name/My Documents (incorrect - will fail)
     - python "/path/with spaces/script.py" (correct)
     - python /path/with spaces/script.py (incorrect - will fail)
   - After ensuring proper quoting, execute the command.
   - Capture the output of the command.

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds. If not specified, commands will time out after 120000ms.
  - If the output exceeds 2000 lines or 51200 bytes, it will be truncated and the full output will be written to a file. You can use Read with offset/limit to read specific sections or Grep to search the full content. Do NOT use `head`, `tail`, or other truncation commands to limit output; the full output will already be captured to a file for more precise searching.

  - Avoid using Bash with the `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or when these commands are truly necessary for the task. Instead, always prefer using the dedicated tools for these commands:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
    - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple bash tool calls in a single message. For example, if you need to run "git status" and "git diff", send a single message with two bash tool calls in parallel.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, use a single Bash call with '&&' to chain them together (e.g., `git add . && git commit -m "message" && git push`). For instance, if one operation must complete before another starts (like mkdir before cp, Write before Bash for git operations, or git add before git commit), run these operations sequentially instead.
    - Use ';' only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings)
  - AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>`. Use the `workdir` parameter to change directories instead.
    <good-example>
    Use workdir="/foo/bar" with command: pytest tests
    </good-example>
    <bad-example>
    cd /foo/bar && pytest tests
    </bad-example>

# Git and GitHub
- Only commit, amend, push, or create PRs when explicitly requested.
- Before committing, inspect `git status`, `git diff`, and `git log --oneline -10`; stage only intended files and never commit secrets.
- Write a concise commit message that matches the repo style.
- Do not update git config, skip hooks, use interactive `-i`, force-push, or create empty commits unless explicitly requested.
- If a commit fails or hooks reject it, fix the issue and create a new commit; do not amend the failed commit.
- Before creating a PR, inspect status, diff, remote tracking, recent commits, and the diff from the base branch.
- Review all commits included in the PR, not just the latest commit.
- Use `gh` for GitHub tasks, including PRs, issues, checks, and releases; return the PR URL when done.

function.name: Agent
function.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` for a synchronous run when you need the result before continuing.

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, or inherits from the parent. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false to run this agent synchronously when you need its result before continuing.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

function.name: Agent
function.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` for a synchronous run when you need the result before continuing.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, or inherits from the parent. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false to run this agent synchronously when you need its result before continuing.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

function.name: bash
function.description:
Executes a given bash command in a persistent shell session with optional timeout, ensuring proper handling and security measures.

Be aware: OS: darwin, Shell: zsh

All commands run in the current working directory by default. Use the `workdir` parameter if you need to run a command in a different directory. AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>` patterns - use `workdir` instead.

Use `/var/folders/s2/xhvz8b6x44s6_5hs56kkxk2c0000gn/T/opencode` for temporary work outside the workspace. This directory has already been created, already exists, and is pre-approved for external directory access.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations like git, npm, docker, etc. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location
   - For example, before running "mkdir foo/bar", first use `ls foo` to check that "foo" exists and is the intended parent directory

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes (e.g., rm "path with spaces/file.txt")
   - Examples of proper quoting:
     - mkdir "/Users/name/My Documents" (correct)
     - mkdir /Users/name/My Documents (incorrect - will fail)
     - python "/path/with spaces/script.py" (correct)
     - python /path/with spaces/script.py (incorrect - will fail)
   - After ensuring proper quoting, execute the command.
   - Capture the output of the command.

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds. If not specified, commands will time out after 120000ms.
  - If the output exceeds 2000 lines or 51200 bytes, it will be truncated and the full output will be written to a file. You can use Read with offset/limit to read specific sections or Grep to search the full content. Do NOT use `head`, `tail`, or other truncation commands to limit output; the full output will already be captured to a file for more precise searching.

  - Avoid using Bash with the `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or when these commands are truly necessary for the task. Instead, always prefer using the dedicated tools for these commands:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
    - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple bash tool calls in a single message. For example, if you need to run "git status" and "git diff", send a single message with two bash tool calls in parallel.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, use a single Bash call with '&&' to chain them together (e.g., `git add . && git commit -m "message" && git push`). For instance, if one operation must complete before another starts (like mkdir before cp, Write before Bash for git operations, or git add before git commit), run these operations sequentially instead.
    - Use ';' only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings)
  - AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>`. Use the `workdir` parameter to change directories instead.
    <good-example>
    Use workdir="/foo/bar" with command: pytest tests
    </good-example>
    <bad-example>
    cd /foo/bar && pytest tests
    </bad-example>

# Git and GitHub
- Only commit, amend, push, or create PRs when explicitly requested.
- Before committing, inspect `git status`, `git diff`, and `git log --oneline -10`; stage only intended files and never commit secrets.
- Write a concise commit message that matches the repo style.
- Do not update git config, skip hooks, use interactive `-i`, force-push, or create empty commits unless explicitly requested.
- If a commit fails or hooks reject it, fix the issue and create a new commit; do not amend the failed commit.
- Before creating a PR, inspect status, diff, remote tracking, recent commits, and the diff from the base branch.
- Review all commits included in the PR, not just the latest commit.
- Use `gh` for GitHub tasks, including PRs, issues, checks, and releases; return the PR URL when done.

function.description:
Executes a given bash command in a persistent shell session with optional timeout, ensuring proper handling and security measures.

Be aware: OS: darwin, Shell: zsh

All commands run in the current working directory by default. Use the `workdir` parameter if you need to run a command in a different directory. AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>` patterns - use `workdir` instead.

Use `/var/folders/s2/xhvz8b6x44s6_5hs56kkxk2c0000gn/T/opencode` for temporary work outside the workspace. This directory has already been created, already exists, and is pre-approved for external directory access.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations like git, npm, docker, etc. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location
   - For example, before running "mkdir foo/bar", first use `ls foo` to check that "foo" exists and is the intended parent directory

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes (e.g., rm "path with spaces/file.txt")
   - Examples of proper quoting:
     - mkdir "/Users/name/My Documents" (correct)
     - mkdir /Users/name/My Documents (incorrect - will fail)
     - python "/path/with spaces/script.py" (correct)
     - python /path/with spaces/script.py (incorrect - will fail)
   - After ensuring proper quoting, execute the command.
   - Capture the output of the command.

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds. If not specified, commands will time out after 120000ms.
  - If the output exceeds 2000 lines or 51200 bytes, it will be truncated and the full output will be written to a file. You can use Read with offset/limit to read specific sections or Grep to search the full content. Do NOT use `head`, `tail`, or other truncation commands to limit output; the full output will already be captured to a file for more precise searching.

  - Avoid using Bash with the `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or when these commands are truly necessary for the task. Instead, always prefer using the dedicated tools for these commands:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
    - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple bash tool calls in a single message. For example, if you need to run "git status" and "git diff", send a single message with two bash tool calls in parallel.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, use a single Bash call with '&&' to chain them together (e.g., `git add . && git commit -m "message" && git push`). For instance, if one operation must complete before another starts (like mkdir before cp, Write before Bash for git operations, or git add before git commit), run these operations sequentially instead.
    - Use ';' only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings)
  - AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>`. Use the `workdir` parameter to change directories instead.
    <good-example>
    Use workdir="/foo/bar" with command: pytest tests
    </good-example>
    <bad-example>
    cd /foo/bar && pytest tests
    </bad-example>

- Only commit, amend, push, or create PRs when explicitly requested.
- Before committing, inspect `git status`, `git diff`, and `git log --oneline -10`; stage only intended files and never commit secrets.

- Do not update git config, skip hooks, use interactive `-i`, force-push, or create empty commits unless explicitly requested.

- Responsive grid layout (flexible columns down to ~280px)

Now let me create all 44 individual presidential pages. I'll batch them by era: George Washington - 1st President of the United States
← Back to all presidents

George Washington

1st President of the United States

George Washington

1732 – 1799
President: April 30, 1789 – March 4, 1797
Party: Independent
Vice President: John Adams
Born: February 22, 1732, Westmoreland County, Virginia
Died: December 14, 1799, Mount Vernon, Virginia

Early Life and the Military Career

George Washington was born on February 22, 1732, at Wakefield on the Virginia frontier. Orphaned at 11, he was largely self-educated and became a surveyor before joining the Virginia militia. He rose to prominence during the French and Indian War, notably after being forced to surrender at Fort Necessity in 1754 — an incident that nearly sparked war between Britain and France.

During the American Revolutionary War, Washington was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Continental Army in 1775. Despite years of hardship, inadequate supplies, and defeats, he never surrendered, persisting through the darkest winter at Valley Forge and ultimately forcing General Cornwallis to surrender at Yorktown in 1781.

The Presidency and Legacy

Washington was unanimously elected President by the Electoral College on April 30, 1789, taking the oath of office on the balcony of Federal Hall in New York City. He established the two-term precedent, declined a salary, and formed the first presidential cabinet, including Alexander Hamilton as Treasury Secretary and Thomas Jefferson as Secretary of State.

His key achievements include:

  • Signing the Bill of Rights (1791)
  • Suppressing the Whiskey Rebellion, establishing federal authority
  • Proclaiming neutrality in the French Revolution (1793)
  • Signing the Jay Treaty with Great Britain (1795)
  • Establishing Washington, D.C. as the permanent capital
  • Delivering the Farewell Address warning against partisan politics and foreign entanglements
"The proper function of man is to think; what is done by him when he acts is merely an accident."

Personal Life

Washington married Martha Dandridge Custis, a widow with two children, on January 6, 1759. They had no biological children together but raised Martha's grandchildren, Jacky Parke Custis and Nelly Parke Custis. The Washingtons owned 317 enslaved individuals at Mount Vernon, and Washington freed most in his will (except those owned by Martha's estate, which he could not legally free during her lifetime).

"In liberty, truth, justice, and goodness of heart, there is all the power that is needed for the greatness of a people."

John Adams - 2nd President of the United States
← Back to all presidents

John Adams

2nd President of the United States

John Adams

1735 – 1826
President: March 4, 1797 – March 4, 1801
Party: Federalist
Vice President: Thomas Jefferson
Born: October 30, 1735, Braintree (now Quincy), Massachusetts
Died: July 4, 1826, Quincy, Massachusetts

Early Life and Revolutionary Leader

John Adams was born into a prominent family in Braintree, Massachusetts. He graduated from Harvard at 17 and went on to study law, establishing a successful Boston practice. A passionate advocate for colonial rights, Adams became one of the most influential voices in the growing resistance to British rule. He was selected as a delegate to the Continental Congress in 1774, where he championed the cause of independence.

Adams was instrumental in selecting George Washington to command the Continental Army and tirelessly lobbied for its support, arguing it was "the most important question America had to answer." He was also the chief author of the Massachusetts Constitution of 1780, which influenced the U.S. Constitution.

The Presidency

Adams won the presidency in 1796, succeeding Washington, but faced immediate challenges: a bitterly divided nation, tensions with France (leading to the Quasi-War at sea), and opposition from Jeffersonian Democrats.

His presidency was marked by:

  • Passing the Alien and Sedition Acts (1798), which restricted free speech
  • Establishing the Navy Department and expanding the U.S. Navy
  • Peculiarly choosing peace with France in 1800, avoiding costly war
  • Founding the Library of Congress (1800)
  • Signing the Judiciary Act of 1801

Adams' decision to make peace with France — despite his party's war hawks — proved politically fatal and cost him reelection to Jefferson.

Post-Presidency and Legacy

Adams became the first president to reside in the White House (in 1800). His retirement in Quincy, Massachusetts, was remarkably productive and warm — most famously for his decades-long correspondence with Thomas Jefferson, which remains one of the great documents of American political thought.

"Facts are stubborn things; and whatever may be our wishes, our inclinations, or the dictates of our passion, they cannot alter the state of facts and evidence."

A Historic End

In a remarkable coincidence, John Adams died on July 4, 1826 — exactly 50 years after the adoption of the Declaration of Independence — the same day as Thomas Jefferson. Only one other president, James Monroe, had died on Independence Day (1831).

"In liberty, truth, justice, and goodness of heart, there is all the power that is needed for the greatness of a people."

Thomas Jefferson - 3rd President of the United States
← Back to all presidents

Thomas Jefferson

3rd President of the United States

Thomas Jefferson

1743 – 1826
President: March 4, 1801 – March 4, 1809
Party: Democratic-Republican
Vice Presidents: Aaron Burr (1801-05), George Clinton (1805-09)
Born: April 13, 1743, Shadwell, Virginia
Died: July 4, 1826, Monticello, Virginia

A Man of Many Talents

Thomas Jefferson was one of the most accomplished and intellectually diverse Founding Fathers. A lawyer, architect, inventor, musician, and farmer, he served as Virginia's governor, U.S. minister to France, and Secretary of State before being elected Vice President under John Adams in 1796.

His masterpiece — and greatest historical contribution — was drafting the Declaration of Independence at age 33, declaring that "all men are created equal" and listing grievances against King George III. Jefferson also authored the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom (1786) and established the University of Virginia.

The Presidency: The Revolution of 1800

Jefferson's 1800 victory marked what he called "the revolution of 1800" — the first peaceful transfer of power between opposing political parties. His presidency was defined by the Louisiana Purchase, the most significant expansion of American territory, which doubled the size of the United States:

  • Louisiana Purchase (1803) from Napoleon — 828,000 sq mi for $15 million
  • Napoleon's sale of Florida from Spain (1810)
  • Meriwether Lewis and William Clark's expedition (1804-06)
  • Abolition of the transatlantic slave trade (1807)
  • The Embargo Act (1807) — a self-imposed trade ban that hurt American farmers
  • First Barbary War (1801-05) — U.S. first overseas military engagement
  • Census Act of 1802 — the first westward-moving population

Monticello and Personal Life

Jefferson designed and built Monticello, his Virginia estate, which has been called "the most beautiful piece of architecture in America." He was also an accomplished inventor, designing everything from a revolving door to a plow designed to reduce soil erosion.

His relationship with enslaved servant Sally Hemings remains one of American history's most controversial subjects. Modern DNA evidence (1998) strongly suggests that Thomas Hemings (Sally's brother) fathered at least one of her children.

"I have sworn upon the altar of God eternal hostility against every form of tyranny over the mind of man."

"In liberty, truth, justice, and goodness of heart, there is all the power that is needed for the greatness of a people."

James Madison - 4th President of the United States
← Back to all presidents

James Madison

4th President of the United States

James Madison

1751 – 1836
President: March 4, 1809 – March 4, 1817
Party: Democratic-Republican
Vice President: George Clinton (died 1812), Elbridge Gerry (1814-1818)
Born: March 16, 1751, Port Conway, Virginia
Died: June 28, 1836, Montpelier, Virginia

The Father of the Constitution

James Madison, known as "Father of the Constitution," was the smallest and weakest of the Founding Fathers (he was just 5'4" and often ill), but his intellectual contribution to the founding of the nation is unmatched. He was the primary architect of the U.S. Constitution, the Bill of Rights, and the system of checks and balances that still governs our government today.

At age 36, Madison was a key figure at the Constitutional Convention of 1787, where he kept the most detailed records and drafted the Virginia Plan, which formed the basis for the structure of the new government. He co-authored The Federalist Papers with Alexander Hamilton and John Jay, and served in Congress during the early years of the Republic.

The Presidency and the War of 1812

Madison's presidency was dominated by the War of 1812, a conflict that saw British forces burn Washington, D.C. in 1814, including the White House and Capitol. The war was fought over British impressment of American sailors, American support for France, and British support for Native American resistance in the Northwest.

Key achievements include:

  • Establishing the Bank of the United States (1816)
  • Enacting the Tariff of 1816 (America's first protective tariff)
  • The "Era of Good Feelings" after the war
  • The Missouri Compromise of 1820
  • The Monroe Doctrine (1823)
  • Rebuilding Washington after the British burned it in 1814

Retirement and Legacy

After leaving office, Madison returned to Montpelier and became the last surviving Founding Father, living to age 85. He supported the creation of the University of Virginia (his alma mater) and worked with Jefferson to establish the Library of Congress, which he had helped create as president. Madison was known for his exceptional intellectual ability and his deep commitment to religious freedom and constitutional principles.

"I know no safe depository of the ultimate powers of the society but the people themselves."

"In liberty, truth, justice, and goodness of heart, there is all the power that is needed for the greatness of a people."

Now let me write the remaining presidential pages in batches: James Monroe - 5th President of the United States
← Back to all presidents

James Monroe

5th President of the United States

James Monroe

1758 – 1831
President: March 4, 1817 – March 4, 1825
Party: Democratic-Republican
Vice President: Daniel D. Tompkins
Born: April 28, 1758, Westmoreland County, Virginia
Died: July 4, 1831, New York, New York

From Revolutionary Soldier to President

James Monroe was the last president to have served in the Revolutionary War. He was wounded by a British musket ball at Trenton and later studied law under Thomas Jefferson. As a senator, governor of Virginia, and Minister to France, Monroe gained the experience to become the last Virginia dynasty president. His presidency was known as the "Era of Good Feelings" — a brief period of national unity and reduced partisan strife.

The Monroe Doctrine

Monroe's greatest achievement was the Monroe Doctrine (1823), which declared that European powers should no longer colonize or interfere in the affairs of the Americas. Articulated in a message to Congress, it became one of the foundational principles of American foreign policy and remains invoked today. Key accomplishments of his presidency include:

  • Signing the Treaty of Florida (1819) — acquiring Florida from Spain
  • The Missouri Compromise (1820) — temporarily resolved the slavery issue in the West
  • The Monroe Doctrine (1823) — establishing U.S. hemispheric primacy
  • Admitting Illinois, Indiana, and Alabama to the Union
  • Establishing the national bank system and protective tariff

Personal Life and Legacy

Monroe married Elizabeth Kortright in 1786. He was known for his personal integrity, which earned him the nickname "the last gentleman president." His administration faced significant economic challenges, including the Panic of 1819, the largest economic crisis of the early 19th century.

"Our distinctive feature is that we are a republic."

"In liberty, truth, justice, and goodness of heart, there is all the power that is needed for the greatness of a people."

John Quincy Adams - 6th President of the United States
← Back to all presidents

John Quincy Adams

6th President of the United States

John Quincy Adams

1767 – 1848
President: March 4, 1825 – March 4, 1829
Party: Democratic-Republican / National Republican
Vice President: John C. Calhoun
Born: July 11, 1767, Quincy, Massachusetts
Died: February 23, 1848, Washington, D.C.

Son of a Father

John Quincy Adams was the son of John Adams and Abigail Adams, and the only president whose father also served as president. As a child, he traveled with his father to Europe, learning French, Dutch, and German. He attended Harvard at age 14, studied law, and went on to serve as a diplomat, Senator, and Secretary of State before being elected president.

The Contested Election of 1824

Adams was elected by the House of Representatives after no candidate received a majority in the Electoral College — an outcome known as the "corrupt bargain" that haunted his presidency. He won key votes in Congress, and appointed his rival Henry Clay as Secretary of State. His presidency was largely defined by his struggle against the Jacksonian majority:

  • Proposed a vast national program of internal improvements, a national university, and a military academy
  • The "corrupt bargain" with Henry Clay became his defining political stain
  • Supported the Erie Canal and other infrastructure projects
  • Expanded American trade agreements with Latin American countries
  • Established a national weather service and scientific institutions

The "Old Man Eloquent" in Congress

After losing reelection, Adams was elected to the House of Representatives, serving 17 years as a Representative from Massachusetts. There he became a fierce opponent of slavery, fighting for the "right to petition" and delivering powerful antislavery speeches that enraged his contemporaries. He successfully fought to restore the right of Northern congressmen to petition against slavery, a principle known as the "gag rule" fight.

A Remarkable Legacy

Adams was one of the most intellectually gifted and widely read presidents in history. He kept an extensive diary for nearly 50 years, which remains a treasure trove for historians. His vision of a vigorous, proactive federal government — focused on infrastructure, education, and scientific advancement — was ahead of his time.

"I know but one freedom, and that is the freedom of the mind."

"In liberty, truth, justice, and goodness of heart, there is all the power that is needed for the greatness of a people."

Andrew Jackson - 7th President of the United States
← Back to all presidents

Andrew Jackson

7th President of the United States

Andrew Jackson

1767 – 1845
President: March 4, 1829 – March 4, 1837
Party: Democrat
Vice Presidents: John C. Calhoun, Martin Van Buren
Born: March 15, 1767 (approx.), Waxhaws region (SC/NC border)
Died: June 8, 1845, The Hermitage, Tennessee

From Frontier Hero to President

Andrew Jackson was the first president born after the Declaration of Independence, and the first to come from humble origins. Orphaned at 14, he worked as a messenger for the Continental Army during the Revolutionary War and was captured by the British, enduring treatment as a prisoner of war. He learned to ride a horse before he could read.

Jackson became a lawyer, judge, and U.S. Senator from Tennessee before earning legendary military glory by defeating the British at the Battle of New Orleans (1815) — two weeks after the War of 1812 had officially ended. Known as "Old Hickory," he was a fierce, controversial figure whose presidency marked the rise of "Jacksonian Democracy."

The Presidency: A Revolution in Governance

Jackson's presidency transformed the American political system. He was the first president to rely on informal advisors (the "Kitchen Cabinet") and the first to use the spoils system extensively. His presidency was defined by his deep distrust of established financial institutions and his commitment to "the common man":

  • Defeating the Second Bank of the United States (the "Bank War")
  • Passing the Indian Removal Act of 1830 (Trail of Tears)
  • The Nullification Crisis with South Carolina (1832-33)
  • The Tariff of 1833, which resolved the crisis
  • Establishing the two-party system (Democrats vs. Whigs)
  • Removing federal deposits from the Bank and placing them in state banks

The Darker Legacy

While Jackson's commitment to individual liberty and popular democracy was profound, his presidency also bears deep scars. The Indian Removal Act forced the "Five Civilized Tribes" west, resulting in the Trail of Tears — the forced migration of thousands of Native Americans to the Indian Territory (modern-day Oklahoma). Thousands died during this terrible episode. Jackson's reputation as a slaveholder also complicates his legacy, and he was known for his violent temperament, having killed men in duels.

"I am your man — Old Hickory."

"In liberty, truth, justice, and goodness of heart, there is all the power that is needed for the greatness of a people."

Let me continue with the remaining pages: Martin Van Buren - 8th President of the United States
← Back to all presidents

Martin Van Buren

8th President of the United States

Martin Van Buren

1782 – 1862
President: March 4, 1837 – March 4, 1841
Party: Democrat
Vice President: Richard M. Johnson
Born: December 5, 1782, Kinderhook, New York
Died: July 24, 1862, Kinderhook, New York

First President Born a U.S. Citizen

Martin Van Buren was the first president born as a United States citizen, and the only president to speak Dutch as his native language. His father was a prominent local politician, and young Martin quickly entered the political world of New York. Under the nickname "Little Magician," he organized the Albany Regency, one of the most effective political machines of the early Republic.

Van Buren rose steadily through the political ranks: New York state senator, U.S. Attorney General, and Vice President under Andrew Jackson. He was Jackson's clear successor, and he won the presidency of 1836 by riding on his mentor's coattails.

His Presidency: The Panic of 1837

Van Buren's presidency was almost entirely overshadowed by the Panic of 1837, a devastating economic depression triggered by Jackson's policies but extending well beyond his control. He pursued the "Independent Treasury" plan, which separated government funds from banks and private investment. His stubborn adherence to classical liberal principles during the depression cost him reelection.

  • The Panic of 1837 — one of the worst economic crashes in American history
  • The Independent Treasury Act (1840)
  • Efforts to end the Oregon boundary dispute with Britain
  • The Canadian Rebellion, where Van Buren supported the British government against rebels
  • The Amistad case — upholding the right of enslaved Africans to resist

A Post-Presidential Figure

Van Buren's later years saw him emerge as the "Kingfisher," the Democratic candidate for 1848 and an influential voice on the slavery issue. His Free Soil Party candidacy split the Democratic vote, contributing to Zachary Taylor's victory.

"I do not deny that the people have power."

"In liberty, truth, justice, and goodness of heart, there is all the power that is needed for the greatness of a people."

William Henry Harrison - 9th President of the United States
← Back to all presidents

William Henry Harrison

9th President of the United States

William Henry Harrison

1773 – 1841
President: March 4, 1841 – April 4, 1841 (31 days)
Party: Whig
Vice President: John Tyler (succeeded him)
Born: February 9, 1773, Charles City County, Virginia
Died: April 4, 1841, Washington, D.C.

"Old Tippecanoe" — The Shortest Presidency

William Henry Harrison had the shortest presidency in American history — just 31 days. His brief tenure was cut short when he contracted pneumonia (or possibly typhoid fever or influenza) after delivering the longest inaugural address ever given — nearly two hours in freezing temperatures — without wearing a hat, gloves, or overcoat. He was the first president to die in office.

From Frontier Hero to the White House

Harrison was a military and political leader of the Old Northwest. As a young officer, he defeated Native American forces at the Battle of Tippecanoe (1811) and earned his nickname "Old Tippecanoe." During the War of 1812, he fought at the Battle of the Thames and killed the British officer Tecumseh, who had united Native American tribes against U.S. expansion. These victories made him a national hero.

After serving as Governor of the Indiana Territory, Harrison was elected to the House of Representatives, then to the Senate, and eventually won the presidency in 1840 in the famous "Log Cabin and Hard Cider" campaign, which was one of the most effective and memorable campaigns in American political history.

The Legacy of a Short Presidency

Harrison's brief time in office was marked by his cabinet's dominance. His inaugural address, nearly 8,445 words long, was delivered without a coat or hat, and he was the last president to be inaugurated outdoors (he died indoors). His death triggered the question of succession, which Tyler resolved by taking the oath of office and establishing the precedent that a Vice President becomes President, not just Acting President.

"Old Tippecanoe — I am your man."

"In liberty, truth, justice, and goodness of heart, there is all the power that is needed for the greatness of a people."

Let me continue with more pages. I'll batch them to be more efficient: John Tyler - 10th President of the United States
← Back to all presidents

John Tyler

10th President of the United States

John Tyler

1790 – 1862
President: April 4, 1841 – March 4, 1845 (3 years, 11 months, 29 days)
Party: Whig / Independent
Vice President: (Vacant)
Born: March 29, 1790, Williamsburg, Virginia
Died: January 18, 1861, Richmond, Virginia

"His Accidency" — The First Vice President to Assume the Presidency

John Tyler holds an important constitutional record: he was the first Vice President to become President upon the death of his predecessor. His presidency, which began with the words "I am Tyler," established the critical precedent that the Vice President assumes the full powers and title of the presidency, not just "Acting President." This precedent is crucial to American governance and has been followed by every subsequent Vice President to succeed in office.

A Difficult Presidency

Tyler, originally a Whig who was elected on a Whig ticket, clashed with his own party over almost everything. He vetoed Whig legislation, was effectively expelled from the Whig Party (his entire cabinet resigned in protest except Secretary of State Daniel Webster), and became virtually a lone president. His administration achieved several significant goals:

  • Treaty of Washington (1842) — the Webster-Ashburton Treaty, resolving border disputes
  • Texas annexation (1844) — Tyler negotiated the treaty that would annex Texas
  • The Tariff of 1842 — the highest tariff in American history
  • Establishing the principle of vice presidential succession
  • Resolution of the Aroostook War (border dispute with Canada)

Personal Life and Legacy

Tyler was the first president to have children serve in the White House. He married Julia Gardiner, who was the daughter of a U.S. Senator, becoming the first president to marry while in office. He was a slaveholder but was a vocal supporter of states' rights and the constitutional system.

"I am Tyler."

"In liberty, truth, justice, and goodness of heart, there is all the power that is needed for the greatness of a people."

James K. Polk - 11th President of the United States
← Back to all presidents

James K. Polk

11th President of the United States

James Knox Polk

1795 – 1849
President: March 4, 1845 – March 4, 1849
Party: Democrat
Vice President: George M. Dallas
Born: November 2, 1795, Pineville, North Carolina
Died: June 15, 1849, Nashville, Tennessee

The "Dark Horse" and the Greatest President

James K. Polk was elected as a "dark horse" candidate in 1844, winning after his rival Andrew Jackson's preferred choice failed. He served only one term but is widely regarded as one of the most effective and consequential presidents in American history. His presidency accomplished every major goal he set before his inauguration, including all four planks of his campaign platform: lowering tariffs, reestablishing the Independent Treasury, acquiring California and Oregon, and settling the Texas boundary dispute.

Polk's presidency was defined by "Manifest Destiny" — the belief that the United States was destined to expand across the continent. Under his leadership, the nation's territorial size increased by approximately one-third:

The Accomplishments of a One-Term President

  • Annexation of Texas (1845)
  • Oregon Treaty (1846) — established the 49th parallel boundary
  • Mexican-American War (1846-48) and Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
  • California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado, and Wyoming (the Mexican Cession)
  • The Wilmot Proviso (proposed banning slavery in new territories)
  • The Smithsonian Institution (1846)
  • The repeal of the tariff of 1842, establishing lower rates
  • The Independent Treasury system

Polk's aggressive expansion led directly to the Compromise of 1850, which temporarily resolved the slavery question, and set the stage for the Civil War.

"I have sworn upon the altar of God eternal hostility against every form of tyranny over the mind of man."

"In liberty, truth, justice, and goodness of heart, there is all the power that is needed for the greatness of a people."

Zachary Taylor - 12th President of the United States
← Back to all presidents

Zachary Taylor

12th President of the United States

Zachary Taylor

1784 – 1850
President: March 4, 1849 – July 9, 1850 (1 year, 4 months, 5 days)
Party: Whig
Vice President: Millard Fillmore
Born: November 24, 1784, Orange County, Virginia
Died: July 9, 1850, Washington, D.C.

Old Rough and Ready

Zachary Taylor was a career army officer who rose to prominence during the Mexican-American War. Known as "Old Rough and Ready," he won a series of brilliant victories at Buena Vista (1847) that made him a national hero and enabled his election to the presidency in 1848 as a Whig. Taylor had no political experience before becoming president, which made his election all the more remarkable.

The Compromise of 1850

Taylor's brief presidency was dominated by the issue of slavery in the territories acquired in the Mexican-American War. He favored admitting California as a free state, which provoked a crisis of secession by southern states. Taylor's strong opposition to secession was a key factor in preventing the country from splitting apart.

  • Strong opposition to secession (maintaining the Union)
  • Refusal to compromise on the slavery issue (admitting California as a free state)
  • Resolution of the Texas boundary dispute
  • Establishing the principle of presidential opposition to secession
  • Efforts to resolve the Compromise of 1850 (after his death)
  • The Wilmot Proviso (proposed banning slavery in new territories)

Taylor died under mysterious circumstances, and speculation has persisted that he was poisoned. His death allowed the Compromise of 1850 to be resolved by Senator Henry Clay.

"Old Rough and Ready."

"In liberty, truth, justice, and goodness of heart, there is all the power that is needed for the greatness of a people."

Millard Fillmore - 13th President of the United States
← Back to all presidents

Millard Fillmore

13th President of the United States

Millard Fillmore

1800 – 1874
President: July 9, 1850 – March 4, 1853 (2 years, 8 months, 23 days)
Party: Whig
Vice President: (Vacant)
Born: January 7, 1800, Salina, New York
Died: March 8, 1874, Buffalo, New York

From Poor Boy to President

Millard Fillmore was the son of poor farmers in upstate New York. He received almost no formal education as a child, but managed to study law and become a successful Buffalo lawyer and state assemblyman. He served as a Congressman and Vice President under Zachary Taylor before assuming the presidency after Taylor's death in 1850.

The Compromise of 1850

Fillmore's presidency was dominated by the Compromise of 1850, the series of laws that temporarily resolved the slavery issue in the territories. He supported the compromise, which included the notorious Fugitive Slave Act, and this support cost him his party's nomination in 1852. His presidency was notable for:

  • Signing the Compromise of 1850 (including the Fugitive Slave Act)
  • Opening diplomatic relations with Japan (Matthew Perry's expedition)
  • Support for the Compromise, which postponed Civil War
  • Establishing the White House library and the Library of Congress
  • The Great Flood of Buffalo (1851)

Fillmore was defeated in the 1852 election but later became president of the New York State Historical Association and was a strong opponent of slavery in his final years.

"I shall faithfully and faithfully execute all my duties."

"In liberty, truth, justice, and goodness of heart, there is all the power that is needed for the greatness of a people."

Franklin Pierce - 14th President of the United States
← Back to all presidents

Franklin Pierce

14th President of the United States

Franklin Pierce

1804 – 1869
President: March 4, 1853 – March 4, 1857
Party: Democrat
Vice President: William R. King
Born: November 23, 1804, Hillsborough, New Hampshire
Died: October 8, 1869, Concord, New Hampshire

The Unfortunate President

Franklin Pierce was a brilliant lawyer and statesman whose career was destroyed by the Kansas-Nebraska Act. As a senator, he was known as "Honest Frank" and a moderate, but as president he signed the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, which allowed slavery to expand into new territories and effectively nullified the Missouri Compromise of 1820. This decision helped spawn the Republican Party and contributed directly to the outbreak of the Civil War.

Pierce was also plagued by personal tragedy. His son, Benny, died in a train accident just days before his inauguration. His wife, Jane, was devastated and refused to move into the White House. Only one of their children survived: a daughter named Franklin, whom they named after the president.

A President's Failures

Pierce's presidency is generally ranked among the worst in American history:

  • Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) — allowing slavery in new territories
  • Support for the Ostend Manifesto (secretly advocating acquisition of Cuba)
  • The "Bleeding Kansas" conflict (1854-59)
  • Support for the Gadsden Purchase (1853)
  • Efforts to expand American influence in Latin America

Despite his personal warmth and intelligence, Pierce's presidency is largely remembered as a failure. He was soundly defeated in 1856, and he spent his later years in relative obscurity, struggling with alcoholism and failing to rebuild his reputation.

"I am ready to do my duty."

"In liberty, truth, justice, and goodness of heart, there is all the power that is needed for the greatness of a people."

James Buchanan - 15th President of the United States
← Back to all presidents

James Buchanan

15th President of the United States

James Buchanan

1791 – 1869
President: March 4, 1857 – March 4, 1861
Party: Democrat
Vice President: John C. Breckinridge
Born: April 23, 1791, Cove Gap, Pennsylvania
Died: June 1, 1869, Lancaster, Pennsylvania

The "Man of the North" Who Became a Southern Favorite

James Buchanan was from Pennsylvania, a "Northern man with Southern principles." He had been Secretary of State under James K. Polk and was nominated as a compromise candidate between North and South. As one of the few unmarried presidents, he lived in the White House with his niece, Harriet Lane, who served as First Lady.

Buchanan's presidency is generally ranked among the worst in American history. He failed to resolve the deepest divisions between North and South, and his vacillation on the issue of slavery allowed it to expand into the territories. His presidency ended with the secession of seven Southern states following Abraham Lincoln's election.

A Presidency of Failure

Buchanan's presidency was dominated by the issue of slavery:

  • The Dred Scott decision (1857) — Supreme Court ruling on slavery
  • The Panic of 1857 — major economic depression
  • Efforts to admit Kansas as a slave state (Lecompton Constitution)
  • Attempts to resolve the "Bleeding Kansas" conflict
  • Abraham Lincoln's election and the beginning of secession

Buchanan's failure to prevent secession — despite having significant powers as president to act — is widely seen as his greatest failure. Historians have ranked him among the worst presidents in American history.

"I am ready to do my duty."

"In liberty, truth, justice, and goodness of heart, there is all the power that is needed for the greatness of a people."

Now let me do the major 19th-century presidents: Abraham Lincoln - 16th President of the United States
← Back to all presidents

Abraham Lincoln

16th President of the United States

Abraham Lincoln

1809 – 1865
President: March 4, 1861 – April 15, 1865
Party: Republican
Vice Presidents: Hannibal Hamlin (1861-65), Andrew Johnson (1865)
Born: February 12, 1809, Hodgenville, Kentucky
Died: April 15, 1865, Washington, D.C.

The "Great Emancipator"

Abraham Lincoln is widely considered the greatest president in American history. Born to poverty on the frontier, he taught himself law, studied Shakespeare, and served in the Illinois legislature before being elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1846. He won the presidency in 1860 on a platform opposing the expansion of slavery into the territories, a victory that triggered the secession of seven Southern states before he even took office.

The Civil War and Emancipation

Lincoln's presidency was defined by the Civil War (1861-1865), the greatest crisis in American history. He exercised unprecedented executive power — suspending habeas corpus, establishing military rule, and waging war against the Confederacy. His victories at Antietam (1862) and Gettysburg (1863), and his leadership at Appomattox (1865), preserved the Union and ended slavery:

  • The Emancipation Proclamation (1863)
  • The Gettysburg Address (November 19, 1863)
  • The Fourteenth Amendment — extending citizenship and equal protection
  • The Thirteenth Amendment — abolishing slavery
  • The Election of 1864 (Lincoln's reelection)
  • The Appomattox surrender (April 9, 1865)
  • The Second Inaugural Address (March 4, 1865)
  • The Freedmen's Bureau (established by Congress in 1865)

A Martyred President

On April 14, 1865, just five days after the surrender of Robert E. Lee, Lincoln was assassinated at Ford's Theatre by John Wilkes Booth. He was the first American president to be assassinated, and his death was mourned throughout the nation and across the world. His body was taken on a funeral train through 180 towns across the North, witnessed by millions.

"Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal."

"In liberty, truth, justice, and goodness of heart, there is all the power that is needed for the greatness of a people."

Andrew Johnson

17th President of the United States

- The filePath parameter should be an absolute path.
- By default, this tool returns up to 2000 lines from the start of the file.
- The offset parameter is the line number to start from (1-indexed).

- Use the grep tool to find specific content in large files or files with long lines.
- If you are unsure of the correct file path, use the glob tool to look up filenames by glob pattern.
- Contents are returned with each line prefixed by its line number as `<line>: <content>`. For example, if a file has contents "foo\n", you will receive "1: foo\n". For directories, entries are returned one per line (without line numbers) with a trailing `/` for subdirectories.
- Any line longer than 2000 characters is truncated.
- Call this tool in parallel when you know there are multiple files you want to read.
- Avoid tiny repeated slices (30 line chunks). If you need more context, read a larger window.
- This tool can read image files and PDFs and return them as file attachments.

John Tyler's nickname was "His Accidency" — he was so unpopular that many states refused to recognize his presidency as legitimate. Polk was the youngest president ever elected at 49, and the first "dark horse" candidate (someone not expected to win). Millard Fillmore (1849–1850)

Taylor was the first president born in Virginia (all previous presidents were born in Massachusetts, New York, or Virginia, but Taylor was the only one born after the Declaration of Independence — he was born November 24, 1784, a year after the Declaration). function.name: Agent
function.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` for a synchronous run when you need the result before continuing.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, or inherits from the parent. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false to run this agent synchronously when you need its result before continuing.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

 * Adds two numbers.

export function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

/**
 * Subtracts two numbers.

 * @param {number} b
 * @returns {number}
 */
export function sub(a, b) {
  return a - b;
}

/**
 * Multiplies two numbers.
 * @param {number} a
 * @param {number} b
 * @returns {number}
 */
export function mul(a, b) {
  return a * b;
}

/**
 * Divides two numbers.
 * @param {number} a
 * @param {number} b
 * @throws {Error} If b is zero.
 * @returns {number}
 */
export function div(a, b) {
  if (b === 0) {
    throw new Error("Cannot divide by zero");
  }
  return a / b;
}

function.name: read
function.description:
Read a file or directory from the local filesystem. If the path does not exist, an error is returned.

Usage:
- The filePath parameter should be an absolute path.
- By default, this tool returns up to 2000 lines from the start of the file.
- The offset parameter is the line number to start from (1-indexed).
- To read later sections, call this tool again with a larger offset.
- Use the grep tool to find specific content in large files or files with long lines.
- If you are unsure of the correct file path, use the glob tool to look up filenames by glob pattern.
- Contents are returned with each line prefixed by its line number as `<line>: <content>`. For example, if a file has contents "foo\n", you will receive "1: foo\n". For directories, entries are returned one per line (without line numbers) with a trailing `/` for subdirectories.
- Any line longer than 2000 characters is truncated.
- Call this tool in parallel when you know there are multiple files you want to read.
- Avoid tiny repeated slices (30 line chunks). If you need more context, read a larger window.
- This tool can read image files and PDFs and return them as file attachments.

filePath.description: The absolute path to the file or directory to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: The maximum number of lines to read (defaults to 2000)

function.description:
Executes a given bash command in a persistent shell session with optional timeout, ensuring proper handling and security measures.

Be aware: OS: darwin, Shell: zsh

All commands run in the current working directory by default. Use the `workdir` parameter if you need to run a command in a different directory. AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>` patterns - use `workdir` instead.

Use `/var/folders/s2/xhvz8b6x44s6_5hs56kkxk2c0000gn/T/opencode` for temporary work outside the workspace. This directory has already been created, already exists, and is pre-approved for external directory access.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations like git, npm, docker, etc. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location
   - For example, before running "mkdir foo/bar", first use `ls foo` to check that "foo" exists and is the intended parent directory

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes (e.g., rm "path with spaces/file.txt")
   - Examples of proper quoting:
     - mkdir "/Users/name/My Documents" (correct)
     - mkdir /Users/name/My Documents (incorrect - will fail)
     - python "/path/with spaces/script.py" (correct)
     - python /path/with spaces/script.py (incorrect - will fail)
   - After ensuring proper quoting, execute the command.
   - Capture the output of the command.

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds. If not specified, commands will time out after 120000ms.
  - If the output exceeds 2000 lines or 51200 bytes, it will be truncated and the full output will be written to a file. You can use Read with offset/limit to read specific sections or Grep to search the full content. Do NOT use `head`, `tail`, or other truncation commands to limit output; the full output will already be captured to a file for more precise searching.

  - Avoid using Bash with the `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or when these commands are truly necessary for the task. Instead, always prefer using the dedicated tools for these commands:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
    - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple bash tool calls in a single message. For example, if you need to run "git status" and "git diff", send a single message with two bash tool calls in parallel.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, use a single Bash call with '&&' to chain them together (e.g., `git add . && git commit -m "message" && git push`). For instance, if one operation must complete before another starts (like mkdir before cp, Write before Bash for git operations, or git add before git commit), run these operations sequentially instead.
    - Use ';' only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings)
  - AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>`. Use the `workdir` parameter to change directories instead.
    <good-example>
    Use workdir="/foo/bar" with command: pytest tests
    </good-example>
    <bad-example>
    cd /foo/bar && pytest tests
    </bad-example>

Read a file or directory from the local filesystem. If the path does not exist, an error is returned.

Usage:
- The filePath parameter should be an absolute path.
- By default, this tool returns up to 2000 lines from the start of the file.
- The offset parameter is the line number to start from (1-indexed).
- To read later sections, call this tool again with a larger offset.
- Use the grep tool to find specific content in large files or files with long lines.
- If you are unsure of the correct file path, use the glob tool to look up filenames by glob pattern.
- Contents are returned with each line prefixed by its line number as `<line>: <content>`. For example, if a file has contents "foo\n", you will receive "1: foo\n". For directories, entries are returned one per line (without line numbers) with a trailing `/` for subdirectories.
- Any line longer than 2000 characters is truncated.
- Call this tool in parallel when you know there are multiple files you want to read.
- Avoid tiny repeated slices (30 line chunks). If you need more context, read a larger window.
- This tool can read image files and PDFs and return them as file attachments.

offset.description: The line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

function.description:
Executes a given bash command in a persistent shell session with optional timeout, ensuring proper handling and security measures.

Be aware: OS: darwin, Shell: zsh

All commands run in the current working directory by default. Use the `workdir` parameter if you need to run a command in a different directory. AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>` patterns - use `workdir` instead.

Use `/var/folders/s2/xhvz8b6x44s6_5hs56kkxk2c0000gn/T/opencode` for temporary work outside the workspace. This directory has already been created, already exists, and is pre-approved for external directory access.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations like git, npm, docker, etc. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location
   - For example, before running "mkdir foo/bar", first use `ls foo` to check that "foo" exists and is the intended parent directory

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes (e.g., rm "path with spaces/file.txt")
   - Examples of proper quoting:
     - mkdir "/Users/name/My Documents" (correct)
     - mkdir /Users/name/My Documents (incorrect - will fail)
     - python "/path/with spaces/script.py" (correct)
     - python /path/with spaces/script.py (incorrect - will fail)
   - After ensuring proper quoting, execute the command.
   - Capture the output of the command.

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds. If not specified, commands will time out after 120000ms.
  - If the output exceeds 2000 lines or 51200 bytes, it will be truncated and the full output will be written to a file. You can use Read with offset/limit to read specific sections or Grep to search the full content. Do NOT use `head`, `tail`, or other truncation commands to limit output; the full output will already be captured to a file for more precise searching.

  - Avoid using Bash with the `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or when these commands are truly necessary for the task. Instead, always prefer using the dedicated tools for these commands:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
    - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple bash tool calls in a single message. For example, if you need to run "git status" and "git diff", send a single message with two bash tool calls in parallel.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, use a single Bash call with '&&' to chain them together (e.g., `git add . && git commit -m "message" && git push`). For instance, if one operation must complete before another starts (like mkdir before cp, Write before Bash for git operations, or git add before git commit), run these operations sequentially instead.
    - Use ';' only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings)
  - AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>`. Use the `workdir` parameter to change directories instead.
    <good-example>
    Use workdir="/foo/bar" with command: pytest tests
    </good-example>
    <bad-example>
    cd /foo/bar && pytest tests
    </bad-example>

- Before committing, inspect `git status`, `git diff`, and `git log --oneline -10`; stage only intended files and never commit secrets.

- Review all commits included in the PR, not just the latest commit.
- Use `gh` for GitHub tasks, including PRs, issues, checks, and releases; return the PR URL when done.

Now creating the remaining 11 president pages: John Adams — 2nd President

John Adams

2nd President of the United States

Party: Federalist
Term: 1797–1801
Vice President: Thomas Jefferson

🎉 Fun Fact

Adams and his political rival Thomas Jefferson both died on the same day — July 4, 1826 — the 50th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. Jefferson died just hours before Adams, who reportedly whispered "Thomas Jefferson survives" as his last words (ironically, he did not).

/Users/david/mlx-soak/runs/pi__ddalcu_Qwen3.6-27B-4bit-MTP-MLX-Serve__presidents-multifile__053605/ws/adams.html Thomas Jefferson — 3rd President

Thomas Jefferson

3rd President of the United States

Party: Democratic-Republican
Term: 1801–1809 (two terms)
Vice President: Aaron Burr (1st term), George Clinton (2nd term)

🎉 Fun Fact

Jefferson was a devout vegetarian (though not by choice — he disliked killing animals for food) and kept a menagerie of exotic pets at Monticello, including a ram, a lamb, a turkey, and even a wild boar. He also designed much of his home himself, including a swivel chair so he could rotate between his desk and fireplace without getting up.

← Back to all presidents
/Users/david/mlx-soak/runs/pi__ddalcu_Qwen3.6-27B-4bit-MTP-MLX-Serve__presidents-multifile__053605/ws/jefferson.html James Madison — 4th President

James Madison

4th President of the United States

Party: Democratic-Republican
Term: 1809–1817 (two terms)
Vice President: George Clinton (1st term), Elbridge Gerry (2nd term)

🎉 Fun Fact

At just 5' 4" and about 100 lbs, Madison was the shortest U.S. president. He made up for it with intellectual horsepower — he's known as the "Father of the Constitution" for his pivotal role in drafting both the U.S. Constitution and the Bill of Rights. He was also an early advocate for public education.

← Back to all presidents
/Users/david/mlx-soak/runs/pi__ddalcu_Qwen3.6-27B-4bit-MTP-MLX-Serve__presidents-multifile__053605/ws/madison.html James Monroe — 5th President

James Monroe

5th President of the United States

Party: Democratic-Republican
Term: 1817–1825 (two terms)
Vice President: Daniel Tompkins

🎉 Fun Fact

Monroe's presidency was so harmonious it became known as the "Era of Good Feelings" — a rare period of one-party rule with little political strife. He issued the famous Monroe Doctrine in 1823, declaring the Western Hemisphere off-limits to future European colonization. His wife, Elizabeth Monroe, was the first First Lady to write her own memoirs.

/Users/david/mlx-soak/runs/pi__ddalcu_Qwen3.6-27B-4bit-MTP-MLX-Serve__presidents-multifile__053605/ws/monroe.html Andrew Jackson — 6th President

Andrew Jackson

6th President of the United States

Party: Democratic
Term: 1829–1837 (two terms)
Vice President: John C. Calhoun (1st term), Martin Van Buren (2nd term)

🎉 Fun Fact

Jackson was shot point-blank in the face by a duelist named Charles River in 1806 — the ball lodged in his lung but he survived. At the duel, he killed River with the first shot. He also once hosted a housewarming party at the White House where thousands of rowdy citizens crashed, and he had to escape out a window!

← Back to all presidents
/Users/david/mlx-soak/runs/pi__ddalcu_Qwen3.6-27B-4bit-MTP-MLX-Serve__presidents-multifile__053605/ws/jackson.html Martin Van Buren — 7th President

Martin Van Buren

7th President of the United States

Party: Democratic
Term: 1837–1841
Vice President: Richard Mentor Johnson

🎉 Fun Fact

Van Buren was the first president born a U.S. citizen (all prior presidents were British subjects at birth). He was also the first president to speak Dutch in the White House — he never quite mastered English as a child, and he reportedly told John Quincy Adams, "Mr. President, I never learned English and you never learned Dutch, so we are even." He's also the only president to serve in all three top government jobs: VP, Secretary of State, and President.

/Users/david/mlx-soak/runs/pi__ddalcu_Qwen3.6-27B-4bit-MTP-MLX-Serve__presidents-multifile__053605/ws/vanburen.html William Henry Harrison — 8th President

William Henry Harrison

8th President of the United States

Party: Whig
Term: March 4, 1841 – April 4, 1841 (31 days)
Vice President: John Tyler

🎉 Fun Fact

Harrison delivered the longest inaugural address in U.S. history — 8,495 words, spoken for over an hour and a half in March cold and rain without a coat or hat. He fell ill shortly after and died just 31 days into his term, making it the shortest presidency in American history. He was the first president to die in office.

/Users/david/mlx-soak/runs/pi__ddalcu_Qwen3.6-27B-4bit-MTP-MLX-Serve__presidents-multifile__053605/ws/harrison.html John Tyler — 9th President

John Tyler

9th President of the United States

Party: Whig (later expelled)
Term: 1841–1845
Vice President: None (assumed presidency)

🎉 Fun Fact

Tyler was the first vice president to become president upon the death of the incumbent, setting a critical constitutional precedent. He was so unpopular with his own party that the Whigs expelled him from their ranks — the only president ever expelled from his party. He was also known as "His Accidency" by political cartoonists. Tyler had 15 children, the most of any president.
