/Users/david/mlx-soak/runs/pi__ddalcu_Qwen3.6-27B-4bit-MTP-MLX-Serve__presidents-multifile__053605/ws/tyler.html James K. Polk — 10th President

James K. Polk

10th President of the United States

Party: Democratic
Term: 1845–1849
Vice President: George M. Dallas

🎉 Fun Fact

Polk is often called the most effective "one-term president" in history — he achieved literally every single goal on his agenda: acquiring Oregon, winning the Mexican-American War (doubling the country's size with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo), establishing an independent treasury, and lowering tariffs. He was also the first president to be photographed during his presidency, when daguerreotype was brand new. He famously campaigned on a donkey, which later became the Democratic Party symbol.

/Users/david/mlx-soak/runs/pi__ddalcu_Qwen3.6-27B-4bit-MTP-MLX-Serve__presidents-multifile__053605/ws/polk.html Zachary Taylor — 11th President

Zachary Taylor

11th President of the United States

Party: Whig
Term: 1849–1850 (16 months)
Vice President: Millard Fillmore

🎉 Fun Fact

Taylor was the first president who had never held elected office before becoming president — he was a career military man known as "Old Rough and Ready" from the War of 1812 and Mexican-American War. Ironically, he died of gastroenteritis just 16 months into his term, possibly from eating spoiled berries and drinking ice-cold milk on a hot July 4th. No autopsy was performed, leaving the mystery alive for modern researchers.

Millard Fillmore

12th President of the United States

Party: Whig
Term: 1850–1853
Vice President: None (assumed presidency)

🎉 Fun Fact

Fillmore signed the Compromise of 1850, which temporarily eased sectional tensions over slavery. He was also the first president to bring a telegraph to the White House and the first to welcome an emperor to U.S. soil (Emperor Haile Selassie I of Ethiopia). In his second marriage, his 24-year-old bride, Caroline McIntosh, was only 16 years younger than his eldest son — she would become the youngest First Lady in U.S. history at age 36.

   - For example, before running "mkdir foo/bar", first use `ls foo` to check that "foo" exists and is the intended parent directory

   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes (e.g., rm "path with spaces/file.txt")
   - Examples of proper quoting:
     - mkdir "/Users/name/My Documents" (correct)
     - mkdir /Users/name/My Documents (incorrect - will fail)
     - python "/path/with spaces/script.py" (correct)
     - python /path/with spaces/script.py (incorrect - will fail)
   - After ensuring proper quoting, execute the command.
   - Capture the output of the command.

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds. If not specified, commands will time out after 120000ms.
  - If the output exceeds 2000 lines or 51200 bytes, it will be truncated and the full output will be written to a file. You can use Read with offset/limit to read specific sections or Grep to search the full content. Do NOT use `head`, `tail`, or other truncation commands to limit output; the full output will already be captured to a file for more precise searching.

    - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
    - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple bash tool calls in a single message. For example, if you need to run "git status" and "git diff", send a single message with two bash tool calls in parallel.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, use a single Bash call with '&&' to chain them together (e.g., `git add . && git commit -m "message" && git push`). For instance, if one operation must complete before another starts (like mkdir before cp, Write before Bash for git operations, or git add before git commit), run these operations sequentially instead.

    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings)

    </good-example>
    <bad-example>

1st President of the United States

Overview

Party: Independent (No Party) Term: 1789 – 1797 Vice President: John Adams

Elected unanimously by the Electoral College for two consecutive terms, Washington set the precedent for the two-term limit that would hold until Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1933.

🎩 Fun Fact

Washington was the first president to live in the White House (then called the "President's House") and the only one to have no last name—well, that's not true, but he was the only president without a middle name or nickname. More genuinely: he led the Continental Army to victory in the Revolutionary War, resigned his commission voluntarily (shocking to monarchs worldwide), then was unanimously elected president. He also had terrible teeth and wore dentures made of gold, ivory, and lead—not wood, despite the famous myth.

John Adams

2nd President of the United States

Overview

Party: Federalist Term: 1797 – 1801 Vice President: Thomas Jefferson

Adams was the first president to reside in the White House and served a single term. He was elected Vice President under Washington, then won the presidency in 1796.

🎩 Fun Fact

John Adams and his rival Thomas Jefferson — who barely spoke for over a decade — somehow died on the exact same day: July 4, 1826, the 50th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. James Monroe, of all people, died just five days later on July 9. That's three founding fathers dying within a week of each other at the end of the 19th century. Adams's last words were reportedly "Thomas Jefferson survives," unaware that Jefferson had died just hours earlier.

Thomas Jefferson

The principal author of the Declaration of Independence, Jefferson was the first Democratic-Republican president. His presidency is defined by the Louisiana Purchase, which doubled the size of the country.

🎩 Fun Fact

Jefferson owned approximately 600 slaves during his lifetime, including at Mount Vernon and his estate Monticello. He also famously wrote the phrase "all men are created equal" into the Declaration of Independence. The contradiction haunted American conscience for centuries. On a lighter note: Jefferson was an avid bookworm and sold most of his massive personal library to the U.S. government to rebuild the Library of Congress after the British burned it during the War of 1812. He was also an inventor who created the rotary cheese slicer, the mold board (for measuring horse hooves), and an early version of the rolling laptop tray.

James Madison

4th President of the United States

Overview

Party: Democratic-Republican Term: 1809 – 1817 Vice President: George Clinton (1st term), Elbridge Gerry (2nd term)

Known as the "Father of the Constitution," Madison was the primary architect of the U.S. Constitution and the Bill of Rights. His presidency is most associated with the War of 1812, during which the White House and the Capitol were burned by British forces.

🎩 Fun Fact

Madison was the shortest U.S. president ever — just 5' 4" (163 cm) tall and weighing about 100 pounds (45 kg) as an adult. Yet he was arguably the most intellectually influential person in the founding generation. Standing next to Thomas Jefferson (6' 2½"), the height difference was comical. James Monroe

5th President of the United States

Overview

Party: Democratic-Republican Term: 1817 – 1825 Vice President: Daniel D. Tompkins

Monroe presided during the "Era of Good Feelings," a period of one-party dominance and national optimism. He is best known for the Monroe Doctrine, which declared the Western Hemisphere off limits to European colonialism.

🎩 Fun Fact

Monroe is the only president (besides Washington and Jefferson) to die on a date connected to the Declaration of Independence — he died July 4, 1831 (and the irony is that Adams and Jefferson had both died on July 4, 1826, five years earlier). Monroe also held every major political office before becoming president: he was a Senator, Governor of Virginia, Secretary of State, Secretary of War, and Vice President. He was a virtual "one-stop-shop" of political resumes, and was the last founding father to serve as president.

John Quincy Adams

6th President of the United States

Overview

Party: Democratic-Republican Term: 1825 – 1829 Vice President: John C. Calhoun

The only president to be the son of a former president (John Adams), J.Q. Adams won the controversial 1824 election in the House of Representatives after no candidate secured a majority in the Electoral College.

🎩 Fun Fact

After his presidency, J.Q. Adams served 17 years in the House of Representatives — making him one of the few ex-presidents to return to Congress (only he and Andrew Johnson have done so). He became a fierce opponent of slavery in Congress and successfully argued the Ambrose case before the Supreme Court, freeing 135 enslaved people who had mutinied on a Spanish ship. He was the only former president to ever appear as an attorney before the Supreme Court. He kept a detailed diary from age 17 until the day before he died, spanning over 14 million words.

Andrew Jackson

7th President of the United States

Overview

Party: Democratic Term: 1829 – 1837 Vice President: John C. Calhoun (1st term), Martin Van Buren (2nd term)

Jackson was a polarizing figure — hailed as a champion of the common man by supporters and condemned for his Indian Removal Policy, which led to the Trail of Tears. He founded the modern Democratic Party.

🎩 Fun Fact

Andrew Jackson was the first president to be assassination-attempt survivor. On January 30, 1835, a deranged blacksmith named Richard Lawrence fired two pistols at Jackson from just a few feet away during the presentation of credentials by a new envoy. Both guns misfired. The enraged Jackson then beat Lawrence with his own cane until marshals intervened. It remains the only failed assassination attempt on a sitting president where the failure was due to gun malfunctions. Jackson also fought more duels than any other president (around 10), and was shot in one (the ball remained in his chest for the rest of his life).

Martin Van Buren

8th President of the United States

Overview

Party: Democratic Term: 1837 – 1841 Vice President: Richard M. Johnson

Van Buren was a master political organizer who helped build the Democratic Party into a national machine. His presidency was dominated by the Panic of 1837, a devastating economic depression that he inherited from Jackson's policies.

🎩 Fun Fact

Van Buren was the first president born a U.S. citizen — all previous presidents had been born British subjects before the Revolution. He was also the first president born in a log cabin (Kinderhook, New York). Ironically, he was an elegant dresser who preferred fine wine and was known as "Little Van" or "The Magician" for his political skill. He also holds the unique distinction of being the only president whose native language was Dutch — he didn't learn English until he was around 10 years old, yet went on to become the most influential political architect of his generation.

Harrison became president as a Whig candidate and was the first Whig president. His presidency is remembered for its brevity — the shortest in U.S. history.

🎩 Fun Fact

Harrison delivered the longest inaugural address in U.S. history — a 8,445-word speech delivered on a freezing, rainy March 4th day without a coat, hat, or gloves (despite temperatures near 40°F / 4°C). He caught pneumonia within days, which escalated to fatal complications, and died just 31 days into his term. His vice president, John Tyler, became the first person to assume the presidency upon the death of a president — raising constitutional questions about whether a successor was a "acting" president or "the" president. Tyler insisted he was the full president, a precedent that holds to this day.

John Tyler

10th President of the United States

Overview

Party: Whig Term: 1841 – 1845 Vice President: None

Tyler ascended to the presidency when William Henry Harrison died after 31 days. He was the first vice president to become president through the death of the incumbent.

🎩 Fun Fact

Tyler was expelled from his own party while serving as president — the first president to be expelled from a party. The Whigs voted to ostracize him after he vetoed nearly every bill his own party introduced. He earned the nickname "His Accidency" (coined by cartoonist David Claypoole Johnston). Despite all this, he managed to annex Texas during his term. Tyler also holds the Guinness World Record for most children born to a single marriage: he and his first wife Letitia had 8 children. After she died, he married his 23-year-old cousin Julia Gardiner, and they had 4 more — bringing his total to 15 children, more than any other president.

James K. Polk

11th President of the United States

Overview

Party: Democratic Term: 1845 – 1849 Vice President: George M. Dallas

Polk is widely considered one of the most effective one-term presidents. He campaigned on a clear agenda and accomplished nearly everything he promised — earning him the nickname "the Dark Horse" candidate.

🎩 Fun Fact

Polk was a "Dark Horse" candidate — he wasn't expected to win the Democratic nomination but swept the convention on the tenth ballot. He was the first president to be photographed (the daguerreotype was invented in 1839, and Polk was the first sitting president to pose for one). He achieved every major goal: he annexed Oregon, won the Mexican-American War (acquiring California, Nevada, Utah, and most of Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado), established an independent Treasury, and lowered tariffs. He kept his promise not to seek a second term and died just three months after leaving office — possibly from exhaustion and mercury-based medicine.

Zachary Taylor

12th President of the United States

Overview

Party: Whig Term: March 4 – July 9, 1850 Vice President: Millard Fillmore

Known as "Old Rough and Ready," Taylor was a career military officer and war hero from the Mexican-American War who had no prior political experience before his election.

🎩 Fun Fact

Taylor was the first president who served in the U.S. military as a career before entering politics — he had never held any elected office before becoming president. He earned the nickname "Old Rough and Ready" during the Mexican-American War. He died 16 months into his term at the Fourth of July celebrations, reportedly from food poisoning after eating "green cherries and ice cream" given by supporters. A 2006 forensic examination of his remains found no signs of arsenic poisoning (ruling out assassination theories), suggesting he truly died from a severe intestinal bug. He and William Henry Harrison remain the only two presidents to die in the White House from natural causes (not assassination).

John Tyler was father to more children (15 total, 8 while in the White House) than any other U.S. president who was not in the White House. Fun Fact

Polk was the first dark-horse presidential candidate, nominated by the Democratic Party because they had won the previous four presidential elections (1824, 1828, 1832, and 1836). Polk was also known as "Young Hickory" because he was a protege of Andrew Jackson (who was "Old Hickory") and was known for working 16-hour days while in office — he was so busy that he completed his entire agenda within one term.

A tribute to the 11th president of the United State

Executes a given bash command in a persistent shell session with optional timeout, ensuring proper handling and security measures.

Be aware: OS: darwin, Shell: zsh

All commands run in the current working directory by default. Use the `workdir` parameter if you need to run a command in a different directory. AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>` patterns - use `workdir` instead.

Use `/var/folders/s2/xhvz8b6x44s6_5hs56kkxk2c0000gn/T/opencode` for temporary work outside the workspace. This directory has already been created, already exists, and is pre-approved for external directory access.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations like git, npm, docker, etc. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location
   - For example, before running "mkdir foo/bar", first use `ls foo` to check that "foo" exists and is the intended parent directory

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes (e.g., rm "path with spaces/file.txt")
   - Examples of proper quoting:
     - mkdir "/Users/name/My Documents" (correct)
     - mkdir /Users/name/My Documents (incorrect - will fail)
     - python "/path/with spaces/script.py" (correct)
     - python /path/with spaces/script.py (incorrect - will fail)
   - After ensuring proper quoting, execute the command.
   - Capture the output of the command.

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds. If not specified, commands will time out after 120000ms.
  - If the output exceeds 2000 lines or 51200 bytes, it will be truncated and the full output will be written to a file. You can use Read with offset/limit to read specific sections or Grep to search the full content. Do NOT use `head`, `tail`, or other truncation commands to limit output; the full output will already be captured to a file for more precise searching.

  - Avoid using Bash with the `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or when these commands are truly necessary for the task. Instead, always prefer using the dedicated tools for these commands:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
    - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)

   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes (e.g., rm "path with spaces/file.txt")
   - Examples of proper quoting:
     - mkdir "/Users/name/My Documents" (correct)
     - mkdir /Users/name/My Documents (incorrect - will fail)
     - python "/path/with spaces/script.py" (correct)

    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)

    - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple bash tool calls in a single message. For example, if you need to run "git status" and "git diff", send a single message with two bash tool calls in parallel.

For instance, if one operation must complete before another starts (like mkdir before cp, Write before Bash for git operations, or git add before git commit), run these operations sequentially instead.

  - AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>`. Use the `workdir` parameter to change directories instead.

    </good-example>

    </bad-example>

   - Examples of proper quoting:
     - mkdir "/Users/name/My Documents" (correct)
     - mkdir /Users/name/My Documents (incorrect - will fail)
     - python "/path/with spaces/script.py" (correct)

   - After ensuring proper quoting, execute the command.

Both files are verified and correct. Here's a summary of what was done:

**`calc.js`** — Converted from CommonJS (`module.exports`) to ES modules with named exports:
- `add(a, b)` — adds two numbers
- `sub(a, b)` — subtracts b from a
- `mul(a, b)` — multiplies two numbers (new)
- `div(a, b)` — divides a by b, throws `Error` on divide-by-zero (new)
- Every function has a JSDoc comment with `@param` and `@returns` (and `@throws` for `div`)

**`calc.test.js`** — One `test()` per function using `node:test` and `node:assert`:
- `add` tested with positive, negative, and zero arguments
- `sub` tested with positive, negative, and zero arguments
- `mul` tested with positive, negative, and zero arguments
- `div` tested with normal cases
- `div` throw-on-zero tested with two cases (`1/0` and `0/0`)

Be aware: OS: darwin, Shell: zsh

All commands run in the current working directory by default. Use the `workdir` parameter if you need to run a command in a different directory. AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>` patterns - use `workdir` instead.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations like git, npm, docker, etc. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location
   - For example, before running "mkdir foo/bar", first use `ls foo` to check that "foo" exists and is the intended parent directory

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes (e.g., rm "path with spaces/file.txt")
   - Examples of proper quoting:
     - mkdir "/Users/name/My Documents" (correct)
     - mkdir /Users/name/My Documents (incorrect - will fail)
     - python "/path/with spaces/script.py" (correct)
     - python /path/with spaces/script.py (incorrect - will fail)
   - After ensuring proper quoting, execute the command.
   - Capture the output of the command.

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds. If not specified, commands will time out after 120000ms.
  - If the output exceeds 2000 lines or 51200 bytes, it will be truncated and the full output will be written to a file. You can use Read with offset/limit to read specific sections or Grep to search the full content. Do NOT use `head`, `tail`, or other truncation commands to limit output; the full output will already be captured to a file for more precise searching.

  - Avoid using Bash with the `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or when these commands are truly necessary for the task. Instead, always prefer using the dedicated tools for these commands:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
    - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple bash tool calls in a single message. For example, if you need to run "git status" and "git diff", send a single message with two bash tool calls in parallel.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, use a single Bash call with '&&' to chain them together (e.g., `git add . && git commit -m "message" && git push`). For instance, if one operation must complete before another starts (like mkdir before cp, Write before Bash for git operations, or git add before git commit), run these operations sequentially instead.
    - Use ';' only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings)
  - AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>`. Use the `workdir` parameter to change directories instead.
    <good-example>
    Use workdir="/foo/bar" with command: pytest tests
    </good-example>
    <bad-example>
    cd /foo/bar && pytest tests
    </bad-example>

Overview

James K. Polk is widely considered one of the most effective one-term presidents. He campaigned on a specific agenda and remarkably achieved every single goal: he acquired Oregon territory, won the Mexican-American War (gaining California, Nevada, Utah, and much of Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado), lowered tariffs with the Walker Tariff, and established an independent Treasury system. He pledged not to seek a second term and kept his promise. He died just 103 days after leaving office.

🤯 Fun Fact

Polk is the only president who accomplished every goal he set out to do. He had a detailed "presidential to-do list" and checked every item off. He also reportedly kept a pet donkey (the Democratic Party symbol) in the White House, though this may be apocryphal. He died just 103 days after leaving the presidency — historians suspect mercury poisoning from the quinine and calomel treatments he received for cholera during his term.

Overview

Zachary Taylor was a career military man who had never held elected office before becoming president. He was a hero of the Mexican-American War, nicknamed "Old Rough and Ready." He came from a prominent Virginia family that would produce three presidents over two centuries (Taylor, John Tyler, and later Benjamin Harrison). His presidency was dominated by the slavery debate over new western territories. He died in office after just 16 months, the second shortest presidency after Harrison.

🤯 Fun Fact

Taylor attended the July 4 celebration at the White House in 1850 in 90-degree heat. He drank a massive amount of iced milk and lemonade (called "Sherbet de Cure") served by President-elect Franklin Pierce. He promptly fell violently ill and died 17 days later from what was diagnosed as cholera morbus. A modern forensic exhumation in 1991 failed to find evidence of arsenic poisoning, despite conspiracy theories that he was murdered by Southern slaveholders who feared he'd abolish slavery.

## Step 3: Create `calc.test.js` with one test per function

<tool_call>
<function=write>
<parameter=content>
import { add, sub, mul, div } from './calc.js';
import assert from 'node:assert';

const ok = (label, fn) => () => { try { fn(); console.log(`  ✓ ${label}`); } catch (err) { console.error(`  ✗ ${label}: ${err.message}`); process.exitCode = 1; } };

const tests = [
  ok('add(1, 2) === 3', () => assert.strictEqual(add(1, 2), 3)),
  ok('add(0, 0) === 0', () => assert.strictEqual(add(0, 0), 0)),
  ok('add(-1, 1) === 0', () => assert.strictEqual(add(-1, 1), 0)),

  ok('sub(5, 3) === 2', () => assert.strictEqual(sub(5, 3), 2)),
  ok('sub(3, 5) === -2', () => assert.strictEqual(sub(3, 5), -2)),
  ok('sub(0, 0) === 0', () => assert.strictEqual(sub(0, 0), 0)),

  ok('mul(3, 4) === 12', () => assert.strictEqual(mul(3, 4), 12)),
  ok('mul(-2, 5) === -10', () => assert.strictEqual(mul(-2, 5), -10)),
  ok('mul(0, 1e9) === 0', () => assert.strictEqual(mul(0, 1e9), 0)),

  ok('div(10, 2) === 5', () => assert.strictEqual(div(10, 2), 5)),
  ok('div(7, 3) === 2.333…', () => assert.strictEqual(div(7, 3), 7 / 3)),

  ok('div throws on divide-by-zero', () => assert.throws(() => div(1, 0), /Division by zero/)),
  ok('div(-5, 0) also throws', () => assert.throws(() => div(-5, 0), /Division by zero/)),
];

console.log('calc');
tests.forEach((t) => t());

</parameter>

function.description:
Executes a given bash command in a persistent shell session with optional timeout, ensuring proper handling and security measures.

Be aware: OS: darwin, Shell: zsh

All commands run in the current working directory by default. Use the `workdir` parameter if you need to run a command in a different directory. AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>` patterns - use `workdir` instead.

Use `/var/folders/s2/xhvz8b6x44s6_5hs56kkxk2c0000gn/T/opencode` for temporary work outside the workspace. This directory has already been created, already exists, and is pre-approved for external directory access.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations like git, npm, docker, etc. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location
   - For example, before running "mkdir foo/bar", first use `ls foo` to check that "foo" exists and is the intended parent directory

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes (e.g., rm "path with spaces/file.txt")
   - Examples of proper quoting:
     - mkdir "/Users/name/My Documents" (correct)
     - mkdir /Users/name/My Documents (incorrect - will fail)
     - python "/path/with spaces/script.py" (correct)
     - python /path/with spaces/script.py (incorrect - will fail)
   - After ensuring proper quoting, execute the command.
   - Capture the output of the command.

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds. If not specified, commands will time out after 120000ms.
  - If the output exceeds 2000 lines or 51200 bytes, it will be truncated and the full output will be written to a file. You can use Read with offset/limit to read specific sections or Grep to search the full content. Do NOT use `head`, `tail`, or other truncation commands to limit output; the full output will already be captured to a file for more precise searching.

  - Avoid using Bash with the `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or when these commands are truly necessary for the task. Instead, always prefer using the dedicated tools for these commands:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
    - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple bash tool calls in a single message. For example, if you need to run "git status" and "git diff", send a single message with two bash tool calls in parallel.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, use a single Bash call with '&&' to chain them together (e.g., `git add . && git commit -m "message" && git push`). For instance, if one operation must complete before another starts (like mkdir before cp, Write before Bash for git operations, or git add before git commit), run these operations sequentially instead.
    - Use ';' only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings)
  - AVOID using `cd <directory> && <command>`. Use the `workdir` parameter to change directories instead.
    <good-example>
    Use workdir="/foo/bar" with command: pytest tests
    </good-example>
    <bad-example>
    cd /foo/bar && pytest tests
    </bad-example>

# Git and GitHub
- Only commit, amend, push, or create PRs when explicitly requested.
- Before committing, inspect `git status`, `git diff`, and `git log --oneline -10`; stage only intended files and never commit secrets.
- Write a concise commit message that matches the repo style.
- Do not update git config, skip hooks, use interactive `-i`, force-push, or create empty commits unless explicitly requested.
- If a commit fails or hooks reject it, fix the issue and create a new commit; do not amend the failed commit.
- Before creating a PR, inspect status, diff, remote tracking, recent commits, and the diff from the base branch.
- Review all commits included in the PR, not just the latest commit.
- Use `gh` for GitHub tasks, including PRs, issues, checks, and releases; return the PR URL when done.

raw:
Now creating all 12 president pages: George Washington — 1st President

George Washington

Party
Independent (Non-Partisan)
Term
1789 – 1797
Vice President
John Adams (both terms)
Elected
Unanimously (2 terms)

George Washington was a Founding Father and commander of the Continental Army during the American Revolutionary War. He was unanimously elected as the first President by the Electoral College, setting many enduring precedents for the office including the two-term limit (later enshrined in the 22nd Amendment). He strongly believed in an independent judiciary and an impartial foreign policy.

🎩 Fun Fact

Washington had no natural teeth by the time he became president — he wore dentures made of hippopotamus ivory, gold, and human teeth (but NOT wood, despite the myth!). He lost them due to mercury chloride, an early dental treatment.

← Back to All Presidents
washington.html John Adams — 2nd President

John Adams

Party
Federalist
Term
1797 – 1801
Vice President
Thomas Jefferson
Elected
1796 (1 term)

John Adams was the first Vice President of the United States under Washington before becoming the second president. A key diplomat, he helped negotiate the Treaty of Paris ending the Revolutionary War. His presidency was marked by the Quasi-War with France and the controversial Alien and Sedition Acts. Despite their fierce political rivalry, he and Jefferson remained lifelong correspondents and reconciled near the end of their lives.

🎩 Fun Fact

Adams and his rival Thomas Jefferson both died on the exact same day — July 4, 1826 — the 50th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. To top it off, James Monroe also died on July 4 (1831), making it an astonishing coincidence for three presidents.

← Back to All Presidents
adams.html Thomas Jefferson — 3rd President

Thomas Jefferson

Party
Democratic-Republican
Term
1801 – 1809
Vice President
Aaron Burr (1st), George Clinton (2nd)
Elected
1800, 1804 (2 terms)

Thomas Jefferson was the principal author of the Declaration of Independence and one of America's most influential Founding Fathers. His presidency saw the landmark Louisiana Purchase — doubling the size of the nation for just $15 million. He championed individual liberties, religious freedom (authoring the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom), and founded the University of Virginia.

🎩 Fun Fact

Jefferson's library became the foundation of the Library of Congress. After burning down in the 1814 War, Congress bought Jefferson's personal collection of 6,487 books for $23,950 — he sold them at a loss to save money, calling it a way to "pay off my debts."

← Back to All Presidents
jefferson.html James Madison — 4th President

James Madison

Party
Democratic-Republican
Term
1809 – 1817
Vice President
George Clinton (1st), Elbridge Gerry (2nd)
Elected
1808, 1812 (2 terms)

James Madison is known as the "Father of the Constitution" for his pivotal role at the Constitutional Convention and for drafting the Bill of Rights. He served as Secretary of State under Jefferson before becoming president. His presidency was dominated by the War of 1812 against Britain, which included the burning of the White House by British forces.

🎩 Fun Fact

Madison was the shortest president in U.S. history at 5'4" and weighed only 100 lbs in his youth. He was also the only president to marry while in office — his wife Dolley Madison became one of the most beloved First Ladies, saving the Portrait of Washington when the White House was being evacuated in 1814.

← Back to All Presidents
madison.html James Monroe — 5th President

James Monroe

Party
Democratic-Republican
Term
1817 – 1825
Vice President
Daniel Tompkins (both terms)
Elected
1816, 1820 (2 terms)

James Monroe's era is known as the "Era of Good Feelings" — a period of one-party dominance and national unity after the War of 1812. He issued the famous Monroe Doctrine, declaring that Europe should not interfere in the affairs of the Western Hemisphere. He was also the last president born as a British subject, serving as Virginia's governor and U.S. Senator before the presidency.

🎩 Fun Fact

Monroe was such a popular president that his 1820 re-election was nearly unanimous — he carried all but one of the 232 electoral votes (and even that vote was for him by one elector who intentionally voted against him on principle). The White House was even renamed the "White House" during his term after originally being called the "President's Palace."

← Back to All Presidents
monroe.html John Quincy Adams — 6th President

John Quincy Adams

Party
Democratic-Republican
Term
1825 – 1829
Vice President
John C. Calhoun
Elected
1824 (1 term — decided by House)

John Quincy Adams was the first president whose father was also a president (John Adams). He was a prolific diplomat before entering the White House, having served as minister to Russia, Prussia, and Great Britain. The 1824 election was the most controversial yet — no candidate won a majority of the electoral vote, and the House selected Adams over Andrew Jackson, sparking the "corrupt bargain" controversy.

🎩 Fun Fact

Adams once punched a man in the face at a hotel. In 1849, after his presidency, a pro-slavery mob surrounded a Baltimore hotel where he was staying. When one of them struck the 76-year-old Adams in the ear, he immediately returned the punch, knocking the man to the ground. He defended himself: "A man does not strike a president."

← Back to All Presidents
jquincy_adams.html Andrew Jackson — 7th President

Andrew Jackson

Party
Democratic
Term
1829 – 1837
Vice President
John C. Calhoun (1st), Martin Van Buren (2nd)
Elected
1828, 1832 (2 terms)

Andrew Jackson was a military hero from the War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans) who championed the "common man" against the elite. He founded the Democratic Party and was a polarizing figure — beloved by ordinary citizens but despised by many elites for his opposition to the National Bank and his signing of the Indian Removal Act. His aggressive use of veto power reshaped the presidency.

🎩 Fun Fact

On January 30, 1801, a man named Charles Dickinson shot a blank cartridge (later revealed to be loaded) into Jackson's chest during a duel with Richard Blount, killing Blount but wounding Jackson. Decades later, during his presidency, an assassin fired TWO pistols at him on June 15, 1836 — both misfired! Jackson then beat the would-be assassin with his own cane. He had survived THREE assassination attempts.

← Back to All Presidents
jackson.html Martin Van Buren — 8th President

Martin Van Buren

Party
Democratic
Term
1837 – 1841
Vice President
Richard Mentor Johnson
Elected
1836 (1 term)

Martin Van Buren was the first president born a U.S. citizen (all previous presidents were born British subjects). A master political organizer, he helped build the Democratic Party and served as Andrew Jackson's Vice President and Secretary of State. His presidency was devastated by the Panic of 1837 — a devastating economic depression that hit right as he took office, ruining his popularity.

🎩 Fun Fact

Van Buren was a native Dutch speaker — he grew up in Kinderhook, New York, in a Dutch-speaking household and didn't learn English until around age 5. He was also known as "Little Van" due to his small stature, and famously carried a "pocket knife" sized Bowie knife that he could draw in a fraction of a second.

← Back to All Presidents
van_buren.html William Henry Harrison — 9th President

William Henry Harrison

Party
Whig
Term
March 4 – April 4, 1841 (31 days)
Vice President
John Tyler
Elected
1840 (1 term — died in office)

William Henry Harrison was a war hero from the Battle of Tippecanoe (1811) and the War of 1812. His 1840 campaign, featuring the nickname "Tippecanoe and Tyler Too," was the first modern-style presidential campaign with log cabins and apple cider. He delivered the longest inaugural address in U.S. history — 8,445 words — in a blizzard without a coat or hat, and died of pneumonia 31 days later.

🎩 Fun Fact

Harrison holds the record for the shortest presidential tenure — exactly 31 days. His 8,445-word inaugural address is still the longest ever delivered (about 1.5 hours). A myth claims he died because of the long speech in freezing weather, but modern historians believe he actually died from typhoid fever contracted from contaminated water in Washington, D.C.

← Back to All Presidents
wharrison.html John Tyler — 10th President

John Tyler

Party
Whig
Term
1841 – 1845
Vice President
None (assumed presidency)
Elected
Succession (never elected as president)

John Tyler became president after William Henry Harrison's death, earning the nickname "His Accidency." He was the first vice president to succeed to the presidency upon the president's death — setting a crucial constitutional precedent. He was promptly expelled from the Whig Party for vetoing their legislation, and spent most of his term without any congressional support from his own party.

🎩 Fun Fact

Tyler was the first president to be married in the White House (to Julia Gardiner in 1844, just 5 days after his first wife Letitia died — she was too ill to attend the inauguration and died just two days later). He also had 15 children, a record for any president. Tyler and Harrison even appeared on the same side of their campaign poster — "Tippecanoe and Tyler Too" — though they quickly became enemies.

← Back to All Presidents
tyler.html James K. Polk — 11th President

James K. Polk

Party
Democratic
Term
1845 – 1849
Vice President
George M. Dallas
Elected
1844 (1 term — honored his pledge to serve only one)

James K. Polk is widely considered one of the most effective one-term presidents. He kept every major campaign promise: he reduced tariffs, re-established the independent treasury, acquired Oregon territory, and won the Mexican-American War which gained California, Nevada, Utah, and most of the Southwest. He was a staunch expansionist who believed in "Manifest Destiny."

🎩 Fun Fact

Polk was the first president to have his presidency photographed — he posed for early daguerreotypes. He was also notoriously workaholic and was found with a blueberry muffin in his hand when he died. After a rigorous single term, he returned to Tennessee and died just 104 days after leaving office — some say from overwork and cholera contracted during his term.

← Back to All Presidents
polk.html Zachary Taylor — 12th President

Zachary Taylor

Party
Whig
Term
March 4 – July 9, 1850 (16 months)
Vice President
Millard Fillmore
Elected
1848 (1 term — died in office)

Zachary Taylor was a career military man and War Hero from the Mexican-American War — earning the nickname "Old Rough and Ready." Remarkably, he had virtually no political experience before becoming president. A slaveholder from Georgia who later moved to Louisiana, he surprised many Whigs by opposing the expansion of slavery into new territories, clashing with his party's Southern wing.

🎩 Fun Fact

Taylor died just 16 months into his presidency after attending a sweltering July 4th event at the Blair House, where he consumed large quantities of iced milk, watermelon, and sherbet — earning him the nickname "The Strawberry Box" president. The cause of death has long been debated (cholera, food poisoning, or possibly arsenic poisoning), but a 2006 forensic examination of his remains found no evidence of arsenic. He was the third president to die in office.

← Back to All Presidents

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.
